description: They say data is the new oil. But unlike oil, they never run out, and become more valuable the more they are encountered.

hero.hook: Facebook can guess that someone is getting married or moving before they even know it.

blocks.text: A phrase has become established since the 2010s: **data** would be “the oil of the 21st century”. The idea is simple: once refined by algorithms, they become the engine of growth and global power.

But unlike oil, a resource that runs out, data is never consumed: it can be copied infinitely, and becomes more valuable as it is combined with other information. Here's why it reshaped the global economy.

The true value of data lies not in a simple list of names or addresses, but in its ability to predict our future behaviors. Every search, every move, every click leaves a trace that technology companies gather to create a very precise portrait of each person.
Facebook can spot a major life change, such as an upcoming marriage or move, before the person involved is even fully aware of it, by detecting small variations in their online habits.

This systematic exploitation of our behavior has given rise to what researcher Shoshana Zuboff calls **surveillance capitalism**: humans are no longer just a customer, they become the raw material of a system that sells predictions to the highest bidder.

The data economy works in a virtuous cycle: the more data a company has, the better its service, which attracts more users, who generate even more data. Artificial intelligence has accelerated this phenomenon: a  algorithm trained on billions of examples becomes more precise and faster to improve than a competitor with limited resources. [[machine learning]]

blocks.caption: Data centers consume as much electricity as entire cities to process these massive flows of information.

blocks.text: These giants,  in the United States and BATX in China, are no longer content with dominating their original sector: they are using their lead in data to expand into health, finance or connected cars, blocking access to innovation in many areas. [[GAFAM]]

sections.title: Why these giants are almost impossible to compete with

blocks.text: Faced with this power, the European Union established  in 2018, a regulation which in theory gives power back to citizens over their own personal information: transparency, right to be forgotten, mandatory consent. [[GDPR]]

Its strength comes from its extraterritoriality: any company that handles the data of European citizens must comply, under penalty of fines of up to 4% of its global turnover. This forced giants like Meta or Amazon to review their practices around the world, making Europe an unwilling global regulator.
Before the GDPR's requirement for clarity, it would have taken an average person around 76 working days to read all the terms of service for the digital services they use in a single year.

Beyond the economy, data has become a tool of power for States themselves, which can use it to monitor their population or guide public opinion. Countries unable to protect their citizens' data risk a form of technological dependence, known as a  breach. [[digital sovereignty]]

The great challenge of the coming decades will be to find a balance between the progress enabled by large-scale data analysis and respect for privacy, an essential condition of individual freedom in an ever more connected society.

Data has become a strategic asset whose value comes from its ability to predict our behavior. This economy favors technological giants that are almost impossible to compete with, to which Europe responds with strict regulation: the GDPR.
